terms.definition: A mapping that brings a source system or specification into RAHP's scenario and assessment vocabulary without replacing the source's authority.
terms.plain_example: A Trust Tasks adapter maps selected source pressures to RAHP patterns.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: A software or human actor that takes actions for itself or for another principal.
terms.plain_example: A software agent requests a credential presentation on behalf of its user.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The conditions under which a risk, control, guardrail or test is relevant.
terms.plain_example: A cross-context privacy guardrail applies only when correlation is not necessary for the declared purpose.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A label for how strong the assurance evidence is, from basic inspection to stronger independent or automated evidence.
terms.plain_example: A2 may require repeatable tests while A0 may only record that no assurance has been shown.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A reusable testable claim about a control or guardrail, including how to test it and what evidence to keep.
terms.plain_example: Try a revoked delegation and confirm the action is blocked.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: Reasoned confidence, supported by evidence, that a system or control behaves as claimed.
terms.plain_example: A replay test and its retained trace support confidence that duplicate execution is blocked.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The party or set of parties for whom a message, credential, proof or authority grant is intended.
terms.plain_example: A proof created for one verifier should not automatically be reused by another.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A recorded event that shows a control, guardrail, decision or override was evaluated or used.
terms.plain_example: The log records that authority was checked and that an override was rejected.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The ability to reconstruct what happened, which rules were used, who acted and what evidence supported the result.
terms.plain_example: An investigator can trace a delegated action back to the principal and active mandate.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A process that establishes which actor, account, key or system is presenting itself.
terms.plain_example: A signature verifies that a message came from a known key.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The legitimate power to make a decision, request an action or change governed state.
terms.plain_example: A valid signature proves who signed; it does not by itself prove that the signer had authority to approve payment.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A decision about whether an actor is allowed to perform a particular action in a particular context.
terms.plain_example: An authenticated agent may still be denied permission to transfer funds.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A collection of scenarios about interactions between two or more systems or specifications. Its provenance and conclusions must be assessed for the composition.
terms.plain_example: A credential and task scenario can test a failure that neither component shows alone.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: The point where one specification, protocol or system relies on facts produced by another.
terms.plain_example: A task engine accepts a credential status result from a separate credential system.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: An action that can materially affect rights, money, access, safety, authority, privacy or an external system state.
terms.plain_example: Revoking access, transferring money or publishing a credential are consequential actions.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The ability to understand, challenge and seek correction or remedy for a consequential outcome.
terms.plain_example: A person can see why access was denied and submit evidence for review.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A rule that ties evidence, authority or a credential to the task, transaction, audience or purpose where it is meant to be used.
terms.plain_example: A witness credential names the trust task that produced it.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A reusable control objective that deployments can apply in their own way.
terms.plain_example: Check current authority at the action boundary.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A new risk or harm introduced or made worse by a control that was meant to reduce another risk.
terms.plain_example: Extra identity checks reduce fraud but may increase exclusion or surveillance.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A deployment-specific measure used to reduce, detect, contain or recover from a risk.
terms.plain_example: A verifier checks status immediately before approving a transaction.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The combined behavior that appears when two or more specifications or protocols are used together.
terms.plain_example: A credential can be valid under one specification but stale under the lifecycle rules of another.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The point where a system changes from gathering information to making or executing a consequential decision.
terms.plain_example: The final approval step before an account is disabled is a decision boundary.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A grant of bounded authority from one actor to another.
terms.plain_example: A person allows an agent to book one hotel within a price limit.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The place in a system where a control or guardrail is actually checked and can stop, change or allow an action.
terms.plain_example: A verifier checks current authorization just before it calls the payment API.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A corpus label describing how its scenarios are grounded in source material, not whether an implementation is safe or has passed tests.
terms.plain_example: A source-informed corpus can suggest useful tests without proving conformance.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: A reusable description of what evidence should be produced, who produces it, how fresh it must be and when it becomes invalid.
terms.plain_example: A revocation propagation trace records when each enforcement point learned about a revocation.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: Information kept to support or challenge an assurance claim, decision or finding.
terms.plain_example: A signed authorization decision record shows what policy and authority were used.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: To stop or refuse a consequential action when a required safety or assurance condition cannot be established.
terms.plain_example: If current revocation status cannot be checked, the verifier defers the high-impact action.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: To continue an action even though a check or dependency failed. This must be explicit when it can create risk.
terms.plain_example: A low-impact read may use a short cached value during a network outage.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The recorded outcome for an earlier finding, such as unchanged, weakened, resolved or superseded.
terms.plain_example: A new normative replay rule changes a replay finding from open to resolved.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A specific observation from a pressure test or security review that needs attention or a recorded disposition.
terms.plain_example: The specification does not say how a user can challenge an adverse decision.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: How recent information or evidence must be for a decision to rely on it.
terms.plain_example: A high-impact action may require status checked within the last minute.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A reusable guardrail that describes what must not be allowed, where it is enforced and what happens on failure.
terms.plain_example: Do not treat a valid credential as permission for an unrelated action.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The catalogue decision that says whether a risk needs a guardrail, needs one only in some conditions, or is adequately handled by controls.
terms.plain_example: A privacy risk may need a guardrail only when cross-context correlation is not necessary.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A rule that blocks or stops an unacceptable state. It is stronger than normal guidance.
terms.plain_example: Do not let a consequential action proceed when current authority cannot be established.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A reusable description of a kind of harm that can appear in many systems.
terms.plain_example: Wrongful exclusion can happen in identity, payment or registry systems.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A bad effect on a person, group, organization or public interest.
terms.plain_example: A person is wrongly locked out of an essential service.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The states an artefact, authority or policy moves through from creation to retirement or invalidation.
terms.plain_example: A credential can be issued, active, suspended, revoked and expired.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The purpose and limits under which an actor or agent is expected to act for a principal.
terms.plain_example: An agent may compare travel options but may not buy one without approval.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The role or actor that is allowed to approve an override.
terms.plain_example: Only the incident commander may approve an emergency continuity override.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A governed exception that allows a normal control or guardrail outcome to be changed by an authorized actor.
terms.plain_example: An emergency override may be allowed only to a named governance role and must be logged.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A high-priority scenario pressure to examine first. P0 is not a measurement of incident severity or probability.
terms.plain_example: Recipient-binding replay is marked P0 for early attention.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: A secondary-priority scenario pressure. P1 is not a statement that harm is impossible or that a system is safe.
terms.plain_example: A less immediate interoperability question may be marked P1.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: The person or organization whose authority, interests or instructions an agent or delegate is expected to serve.
terms.plain_example: A traveller is the principal when a personal agent books on the traveller’s behalf.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A system state that a guardrail says must not be entered or continued.
terms.plain_example: A payment proceeds even though required authority cannot be established.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The person, group or institutional interest that a guardrail is meant to protect.
terms.plain_example: Privacy is the protected interest behind a guardrail against unnecessary disclosure.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: Information about where an artefact, action, decision or claim came from and how it changed over time.
terms.plain_example: A delegation trace shows which principal granted which delegate which scope.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The stated reason for collecting information, making a decision or performing an action.
terms.plain_example: A credential is requested to confirm age, not to build a marketing profile.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A new review performed because the target, evidence, threat model or operating context has changed.
terms.plain_example: A specification changes its revocation rules, so earlier findings are checked again.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A proposed action to reduce a finding or risk.
terms.plain_example: Require a fresh authority check immediately before a destructive action.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A process that can correct, compensate for or otherwise remedy a harmful or incorrect outcome.
terms.plain_example: A wrongly excluded user can appeal and have access restored.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The action taken to correct or reduce the effect of a harmful or incorrect outcome.
terms.plain_example: A registry corrects an entry and notifies affected relying parties.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: The risk that remains after controls and guardrails are applied.
terms.plain_example: A cached status check lowers outage risk but still leaves a short stale-state window.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A stated event that should cause an earlier assurance result or finding to be checked again.
terms.plain_example: Retest when the specification changes its authorization model.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A governed act that ends previously granted authority, status or validity.
terms.plain_example: A principal revokes an agent’s authority to make purchases.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A governed decision to live with a known residual risk for a stated period and reason.
terms.plain_example: A deployment accepts a low-impact availability risk until a replacement service is ready.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A reusable failure mechanism that can appear in more than one deployment or specification.
terms.plain_example: A system may mistake proof of identity for permission to act.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A possible way a specific deployment can cause harm or fail to meet its goals.
terms.plain_example: A registry may keep an old key after it should have been removed.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: An evidence grade for a working pressure-test hypothesis where a source-grounded normative claim has not been established.
terms.plain_example: A preliminary interface receives a scenario to explore before its specification is complete.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: A collection of domain-specific scenarios linked to reusable scenario patterns. A corpus suggests what to test, not what passed.
terms.plain_example: The Trust Tasks corpus lists possible failure situations for task workflows.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: A reusable kind of pressure or failure possibility that can be tested in many systems.
terms.plain_example: Replay of a valid proof is a pattern that may appear in several corpora.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: A situation or condition used to ask what a system should do under pressure. A scenario is not evidence that a failure happened.
terms.plain_example: A signed request might reach the wrong recipient.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: The boundary of what an authority, control, assessment or claim applies to.
terms.plain_example: A delegation may allow read access to one record for one hour.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: An evidence grade used when scenarios draw on known source semantics without claiming a complete pinned normative baseline.
terms.plain_example: A scenario is based on published design concepts but not a complete frozen text.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: A declared source revision used when preparing an adapter. A symbolic or descriptive value is not an immutable commit identifier.
terms.plain_example: A full commit SHA can identify the revision of a specification used for review.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: An evidence grade used when an adapter declares reviewable grounding in pinned source material. It does not certify the target.
terms.plain_example: A scenario cites a checked specification revision, but still needs execution evidence.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP readers in simple English; scenario corpus guidance issue

terms.definition: Old information that no longer reflects the current authority, status, policy or system condition.
terms.plain_example: A cached registry entry still points to a key that has been revoked.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.

terms.definition: A governed temporary stop that may later be lifted without creating a new grant from scratch.
terms.plain_example: A credential is suspended during an investigation and later restored.

source.note: Definition written for RAHP in simple English.
